This case study presents the Discovery Findings report Automagic delivered to Hunter Executive, with commercial terms removed. The PESA platform it proposed was then built and rolled out in three waves.

Section 01

Executive summary

Discovery found that Hunter Executive's consultants spend much of their time gathering and re-gathering intelligence that never accumulates. Research, enrichment, prioritisation, outreach, meeting follow-up and proposals are done by hand, consultant by consultant, outside the CRM. We recommend building PESA, a governed AI operating layer on top of the Hunter CRM, and delivering it in three waves over six months.

What we found. Twenty findings fall into seven themes. The five with the widest impact:

  • Research is manual and spread across LinkedIn, Crunchbase, news and contact tools, with no single intelligence layer.
  • Accounts, leads and candidates are judged by individual instinct rather than a consistent score.
  • Mandate signals such as executive moves, funding rounds and hiring surges are spotted late or missed.
  • Relationship health is not measured, so key relationships decay unnoticed and warm introduction paths stay hidden.
  • Each consultant works to their own rules, and nothing they learn is captured for the firm.

What we propose. PESA gives every consultant a personal AI assistant that sits on shared firm-wide rules, memory and data. Twelve specialist agents in four suites (Sales & Marketing, Executive Search, Relationship Intelligence, Operations) do the work. Placement Radar is the prospecting front end. Hunter's CRM stays the system of record.

How we deliver it. Stage 1 runs for six months in three waves. Wave 1 lays the platform and ships the four quickest agents. Wave 2 adds signals, candidate research, relationship scoring and automation. Wave 3 adds sourcing, outreach and ecosystem intelligence. Stages 2 and 3 then turn the data PESA collects into firm-specific intelligence.

The case. Stage 1 returns about 7 hours a week to each of 12 users and about three extra mandates a year, and on expected assumptions pays back in about 12 months. The engagement is a hybrid of a Fractional Transformation Lead, a monthly consultancy fee and a fixed cost per agent; Hunter owns what is built and pays providers directly.

Section 02

Discovery scope and approach

Discovery covered Hunter's full commercial cycle, from first contact with a prospect to an active client relationship, and the executive search delivery that sits inside it.

  • Duration: four weeks.
  • People: 10 interviews covering the managing partner, senior consultants, the research lead, business development, and operations and finance. All 12 consultants and researchers gave weekly time estimates by activity.
  • Workflows: four walkthroughs of live work: a new lead to first meeting, an opportunity to proposal, a search from brief to shortlist, and assignment opening to invoice.
  • Systems and data: a review of the Hunter CRM data model and pipeline, email and calendar use, and an audit of the external tools and AI services consultants use today.
  • Method: we mapped each workflow step, measured where time goes and where information is lost, scored AI readiness, and traced each problem to a root cause before designing any solution.

Section 06

Proposed solution: the PESA platform

PESA (Personal Executive Search Assistant) is a governed AI operating layer that sits on top of the Hunter CRM. Every consultant gets their own PESA; all PESAs share one set of firm rules, one data layer and one library of specialist agents. The CRM remains the system of record.

Requests flow down from each consultant's PESA through shared rules and agents to the data layer; results and actions flow back into the Hunter CRM.

A PESA for every consultant

Each consultant works through a private AI assistant that knows their assignments, clients, candidates, preferences and history. It answers questions, plans searches and campaigns from a plain-language brief, and calls the right agents to do the work. It replaces public AI tools with one the firm controls (F17).

Five core systems behind every PESA

SystemWhat it doesManaged byShared or personal
Management LogicFirm rules, policies, scoring logic and governanceManagement, through a configuration consoleShared
Workflow OrchestrationReads each request, picks the right suite, agents and data, plans and runs the steps, returns the resultManagement, through workflow rules and prioritiesShared
Human Feedback & ReinforcementLearns from what consultants accept, reject, edit and override, and from outcomesSystem, with management visibilityShared learning
Memory & ContextStores history, relationships, interactions and preferencesSystem, under data and retention policiesPersonal per consultant
AI ModelThe underlying language models that reason and writePlatform team: model choice, prompts, evaluationShared

The PESA Management Agent

Management sets firm-wide rules once: scoring logic, workflow rules, outreach tone, approval requirements, automation limits and compliance boundaries. The Management Agent turns each change into a draft, simulates its impact, and publishes it only after human approval, with version control and rollback. Every PESA then works inside those rules (F19).

Data, Shared Intelligence & Communication Runtime

One shared layer connects PESA to external data and communication providers: Zugi DIC, LinkedIn data, Crunchbase, SignalHire, Unipile, Revscale, Microsoft Graph and Google. Each integration is built once and reused by every agent, so later agents are faster and cheaper to build (F1, F2, F7, F20).

Operational Execution Layer and CRM integration

PESA acts, not just advises: it creates and updates CRM records, sends emails and messages, schedules meetings, creates tasks, generates documents and triggers workflows, escalating for approval where the rules require it. Intelligence actions (research a company, score an opportunity, generate a meeting brief, recommend candidates, draft a proposal) are available inside the CRM screens (F13, F15, F16).

Placement Radar

Placement Radar is the prospecting front end: natural-language campaigns, unified search across companies and people, dynamic lists that refresh themselves, radar alerts on signals, intelligence profiles, and one-click export of leads, contacts and candidates to the CRM (F4, F5, F6, F8).

The AI Agent Library

Twelve reusable agents in four suites do the specialist work: Sales & Marketing (Lead Intelligence, Account Prioritization, Outreach), Executive Search (Sourcing, Candidate Research, Fit Assessment), Relationship Intelligence (RelationshipScore, Ecosystem Intelligence, Next-Best-Action) and Operations (Meeting Intelligence, Proposal Generation, Workflow Automation). Consultants never pick an agent; they ask their PESA, and orchestration routes the work. Part three, after the proposal, summarises each agent and gives its full specification, and Appendix A maps every finding to the agent that answers it.

Section 07

Prioritisation

We scored each agent on its value to Hunter (how many findings it answers and how directly it affects time saved or mandates won) and on build effort. The result sets the order of the waves.

Wave 1 takes the quick wins plus Fit Assessment. Next-Best-Action waits for Wave 2 because it needs relationship scores, and Candidate Research joins it there alongside Lead Intelligence. The enablers also come in Wave 2 because later agents rely on them. Major builds come last, once the data runtime and relationship data are in place.

Section 08

Roadmap

Stage 1 is delivered in three two-month waves, so consultants use real tools from the end of month 2 and each wave builds on the data and integrations of the one before.

Why this order. Wave 1 lays the platform and ships the four agents that are quickest to build, cheapest to run and work mostly from Hunter's own data. Wave 2 adds the agents that need external signals, enrichment and relationship data. Wave 3 brings the heaviest integrations (LinkedIn data, Unipile, Revscale, Crunchbase) and the agents that rely on relationship scores and enriched profiles built earlier.

Capacity. The platform and 12 agents add up to roughly 32 to 49 build weeks. Fitting them into six months means running two build tracks in parallel from Wave 2.

After Stage 1

StageWhat it addsIndicative effort
Stage 2: Organisational intelligenceTelemetry on every workflow, a relationship graph, workflow optimisation, multi-agent coordination, governed semi-autonomous workflowsAbout 27 weeks of capabilities, built alongside agent use
Stage 3: Proprietary executive-search intelligenceHunter's own ranking, placement prediction and workflow models, trained on the data Stages 1 and 2 collectAbout 32 weeks of capabilities

Stage 2 and 3 figures are directional and will be scoped at the end of Stage 1, once real usage data exists.

Section 09

Measuring success and ROI

At full adoption, PESA is expected to give back about 3,900 consultant hours a year and to cut the time spent on the five most time-heavy activities by about a third. It is also expected to add about three mandates a year. On expected assumptions, Stage 1 pays back in about 12 months and returns about 1.9 times its cost over two years. This section sets out each predicted return, how it is measured and when.

How ROI is calculated

ROI = (value of time returned + fee income from attributed mandates − total Stage 1 cost) ÷ total Stage 1 cost

  • Value of time returned = hours saved per user × active users × working weeks × loaded hourly cost.
  • Fee income = mandates attributed to PESA × actual fee.
  • Total cost = build, monthly fees, running costs and third-party data.

Time returned is capacity rather than cash, so it is reported separately from fee income. Hunter sees the return both with and without it.

Attribution rule

A mandate counts towards PESA when the CRM shows that a PESA signal, Placement Radar alert or Next-Best-Action recommendation led to contact with that client in the 90 days before the mandate opened. The PESA product owner confirms each one at the monthly steering meeting.

Section 11

Stage 1 scope and success criteria

In scope

  • PESA runtime with a personal PESA for every consultant, including memory, history and preferences
  • Shared Control Plane and the PESA Management Agent
  • Workflow orchestration, human feedback capture and operational telemetry
  • Data, Shared Intelligence & Communication Runtime, with the providers each agent needs
  • Hunter CRM integration: embedded intelligence actions, record updates, Microsoft email and calendar
  • Placement Radar
  • All 12 agents, delivered across the three waves
  • Testing, consultant onboarding and tuning in each wave

Out of scope for Stage 1

  • Stage 2 organisational intelligence (relationship graph infrastructure, semi-autonomous orchestration, workflow optimisation models)
  • Stage 3 proprietary models
  • Changes to the Hunter CRM's own data model beyond what the integration needs
  • Third-party subscriptions and usage fees, which Hunter contracts and pays directly

Success criteria

  • Every consultant can use their PESA for research, briefs, reports and recommendations on demand.
  • Management can change scoring, workflow and communication rules through the Management Agent, with approval and version history.
  • Each wave's agents are live, return results inside the CRM, and capture consultant feedback.
  • Intelligence and actions write back to the Hunter CRM without manual re-entry.
  • Placement Radar campaigns, dynamic lists and alerts run and export to the CRM.
  • The KPI targets for month 6 in the operating model section are met.
